A somewhat naive anti-surveillance game when it comes to messaging, but considering I'm stating this with hindsight and the many things that both happened and have been revealed since 2016 and the unimpeded expansion of mass surveillance, the naivete is only seen now. Otherwise, an interesting investigation game, though there were several moments that had me annoyed as I would have conflicting datachunks that actually didn't change anything, and simultaneously inoffensive-looking information that would flip the whole plot. 
I think, as a concept, Orwell is great, but the slightly railroad-y execution somewhat holds it back from being genuinely great. Leaving more autonomy for the player to figure things out themselves and go after red herrings or get stuck in logical loops and unimportant information would improve the gameplay. In fact, Orwell does exactly this in the last act by limiting the amount of information that can be processed. 
Nonetheless, I recommend it for the concept and the feeling of being a government spook.

While this game came out almost a decade ago, it seems to be more relevant than ever.

The main objective of the game is to collect information on persons of interest by scrubbing through documents, websites, and other types of media. This will then impact how the narrative moves forward.
The gameplay itself is very light. Because it’s a very narrative focused game, most of the actions are the choices that we make, to either share or not the information we find about the suspects. And of course there is also a lot of reading to be done.

With this type of game, I always feel like there is a point where the player can find links/relations or connections that are not considered as valid until the game says so. I know it’s difficult to account for all possible options or outcomes, but it does break the immersion a bit when it happens.
Having said that, I do feel like the systems in this game are all integrated in a very seamless way. It’s very easy to understand what is relevant or not (even if it can be a bit restrictive sometimes).

One of the few improvements I can think of is an even faster speed for the text messages.

In the end, even if it’s not a long game, it can get quite heavy. I still recommend it as I can see myself replaying this at some point in the future.

Interesting, compelling, and flawed. Contrary to some negative reviews I don't mind the format of Orwell being a linear visual novel, sometimes the best way to tell a complicated story is to tell it simply, and for what it's worth, it works well as long as Orwell is telling the story it thinks it is. 

With that being said, Orwell pulls its biggest punch on its lynchpin issue concerning its closing question on a terrorist attack you've been investigating from the beginning of the story, where, when circling back at the climax, Orwell thinks it's asking you a sensible question. Would I condemn the use of Orwellian nation state surveillance in the face of what we've learned during the story? 

Of course it's something I condemn, we've all a right to privacy.

But in order to answer the question as Orwell wants to phrase it, i found myself being really frustrated with how the game allows you to give your answer, and i'm really disappointed with what feels like really negligent storytelling. 

Orwell isnt as mature as it thinks it is. At the crux of it, Orwell isn't asking you to measure freedom against safety, It asks would you rather be a bootlicker to solve a terror attack killing several and wounding others, or let the perpetrators off because the developers skipped watching minority report?

We've a right to live free from terror, and the real fault of Orwell is that it ends up presenting terror and surveillance as equivalent issues rather than being in tension with one another. You're not asked what would you be willing to do to prevent an act of terror, it's already happened, people have died.

That Orwell also asks if you would like to give the system a middle finger by way of a Watergate sidestep to, again, apprehending conspirators / co-conspirators to a terror attack seems to be completely missing the point.

Am I missing things and details here? Almost certainly, there are a few different endings and granular differences depending on your choices throughout the story that paint a different picture. But for me, Orwell treats 1984 as the only book on the shelf.

Orwell
.
A surprisingly cool game where we scroll through the browser to investigate various incidents, while we work for the government.
"The Orwell Ethical Codex dictates that investigators - like yourself - are the only ones allowed to access the documents of target persons.
Your primary job is to provide information you deem important. NEVER give away incorrect or misleading data."
.
Controls:
Point and click, browser interface
.
Mechanics and features:
Browse The National Beholder.
Open the "Unknown Person" files
The Profiler holds all known information on those we investigate.
The highlighted elements in the record are pieces of data that are able to be extracted. 
We call these elements "Datachunks."
Hovering over Datachunks will reveal their relevance to the case, and any connections or information it may influence.
Drag and drop all Datachunks from the police database into a profile to upload them to our servers.

I was in a bit of a point and click achievement hunting mood, so decided to finally open this up. I always liked the idea and, given the current state of the internet and world as I write this, it felt only right.

It's a simple game, but I can't deny it's executed pretty well. Even the style of it gives off his dystopian "clean government, dirty acts" feel. And while I did know some of the plot beats (I'd read achievement guides to see if I could 100% it. I can, it's easy to, little slow, and I'm fine with spoiling things for myself), the crazy part is it didn't impact them. I didn't know how my acts would play out, only a handful of them. And I found myself cursing out my bosses because of what they did. Activist I feel isn't violent as she was found, curled up, crying in a protest? Still arrested. Woman clearly trying to care for her son and unable to find work due to a crushing system? Shot (non-fatally, at least). Me trying to properly profile folk, knowing the difference between good and evil? Files get leaked, I get new masters who want me to do worse things.

But that's how dystopian Orwellian societies work, isn't it? Good intention, horrific results. A woman was shot despite me constructing a profile of a hard done to veteran. A man was arrested despite me accepting he'd matured since his rebellious college years. Bad things still happened, all in the world where the government had eyes everywhere, where I was trying my best to provide accurate information that focused on the facts and not presumptions like my bosses' had. And I genuinely got annoyed at them for not listening, even knowing that it was just text on screen, not a real person.

It really hit the mark with what it was going for and, more horrifyingly, showed similarities to the world we live in right now. It's, unfortunately, aged like wine...

A lightweight and interesting software title. "Orwell" is more of an interactive visual novel than a game, but tells a story well enough and the 2-4 hour playtime does not overstay too long. The plot is clear from the description and the marketing on Steam's storefront is accurate for what is offered - a tale of dystopia and hyper-surveillance where Your Choices Matter.

Much like "Papers, Please", there is a certain heroic conceit in an everyman investigator charting the path of the Nation, but the player will face real and weighty decisions with far-reaching consequences. By the mid-game, regular questions of guilt based on partial or contradictory evidence emerge and it will be up to you to decide what goes into the report and what does not. It can feel a little incomplete to mete out justice based on little more than social media posts and clipped messages from dubious surveillance, but I'll give a pass to the limited scope of the title because it is presented well and succeeds at reinforcing the message that privacy is complicated and imperfect.

The story also works well enough and there's some refreshing twists and dilemmas that keeps the plot intriguing so long as the player keeps up the tempo. I still feel like the later release of "Hypnospace Outlaw" is a better title in this game genre, but the commentary from "Orwell" about both security and authority are better storytelling than "Hypnospace" and does not disappoint. If you are like me then you'll only play it once and not again, but it's worth the $3 (USD) on sale to experience it and, if you're a fan of "1984", then this little simulation will fit you like a glove.

TL;DR: Great for the most part. An intriguing mystery, in-depth characters, very unique gameplay that I heavily enjoyed. Political commentary is heavy-handed but remains interesting, as most characters are morally grey. Great except the ending.

First issue: the late-game twist. I won’t spoil details, but I will talk about the structure of a major late-game twist. I've played this game through 3 times now, and each time the final twist comes out of nowhere. It has foreshadowing in the same way that me saying "you're stupid" foreshadows that I'm going to stab you.
People justify it by making these massive lists of all these barely noticeable details that come together to hint at the idea that "hey, [character] may not be a great person". And then the game jumps from that to terrorism.
Oh, and a lot of the foreshadowing would only come if people made specific decisions. Certain routes would make the twist (which doesn't change) make more or less sense.
The fact that some people think it makes sense and that some people suspected it while playing means that it functionally can't be that bad. To some degree, it makes sense. It did [i]not[/i] land for me though.

Second issue: moral flattening. I noticed something as I progressed through the endings. A bit more spoilery here, but again no specifics. Throughout the game, most characters are morally dubious. Even when you've beaten the game, you'll likely have mixed opinions of a lot of the characters. However, once you reach endings that reveal a bit more information, it becomes clear that there's a real "These people were right the whole time and these people are wrong and kick puppies" mindset. They can't let their actions through the story speak for themselves. There has to be a reveal that the bad guys were doing even worse secret stuff and are unequivocally bad and the good guys are all vindicated.

Get the game though. Two things about the ending miffed me a bit, but I still had a heck of a lot of fun.
